selection.method: highest remaining verified actor-primary profiles after Batch 19

profiles.name: Howard Da Silva
profiles.excerpt: Howard Da Silva brought a powerful stage voice, radio-directing experience and a politically turbulent screen career into the repertory of CBS Radio Mystery Theater.
profiles.bio_html:
Howard Da Silva was born Howard Silverblatt in Cleveland in 1909 and trained for the stage after working in industry. He became a major Broadway actor, creating roles in The Cradle Will Rock, Oklahoma! and later 1776, where his Benjamin Franklin became one of his signature performances.

Radio was important early as well as late in his career. Da Silva worked in WPA-era broadcasting and recalled directing weekly radio series before Hollywood, then returned decades later as a regular member of CBS Radio Mystery Theater. That earlier directing work is substantial enough to remain a second professional category.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves 22 CBS Radio Mystery Theater performances credited to Da Silva, documenting his return to microphone drama after decades on stage and screen.

profiles.name: Joan McCall
profiles.excerpt: Joan McCall combined acting with a substantial career as a screenwriter and producer, while radio made her a regular voice on Sears Radio Theater.
profiles.bio_html:
Joan McCall was born in Kentucky in 1940 and built a career across theatre, film, television and radio. Her acting work included Broadway and feature films, but she also developed into a prolific professional writer.

McCall wrote hundreds of television scripts, including work for major daytime serials, and also worked as a film producer. Radio listeners heard her repeatedly on Sears Radio Theater, where experienced screen and stage performers returned to anthology drama during the late 1970s.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves 22 Sears Radio Theater performances credited to McCall. Her writing and producing careers are retained as genuine second professional branches alongside acting.

profiles.name: Richard Hamilton
profiles.excerpt: Richard Hamilton was a New York stage and screen character actor whose radio work became strongly associated with X Minus One.
profiles.bio_html:
Richard Hamilton built a long career in theatre, film and television and remained closely connected to the New York acting community. His later screen work included The Hospital, Pale Rider and Men in Black.

Radio made especially strong use of Hamilton in science fiction. He appeared repeatedly on X Minus One, where actors had to move quickly among scientists, officials, ordinary citizens and speculative characters in adaptations of major genre writers.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves 21 X Minus One performances credited to Hamilton and one Dimension X appearance. Science-fiction radio is therefore the clearest surviving GRH concentration of his microphone work.

profiles.name: Edmond MacDonald
profiles.excerpt: Edmond MacDonald was a versatile radio character actor whose credits crossed Box 13, FBI drama, suspense and several major detective series.
profiles.bio_html:
Edmond MacDonald belongs to the professional radio repertory whose surviving cast record is stronger than later personal biography. His work places him repeatedly inside crime, suspense and detective production during the late 1940s and 1950s.

MacDonald appeared on Box 13, This Is Your FBI, The Whistler and Yours Truly, Johnny Dollar, while anthology and private-eye programs used him for additional changing roles. The breadth of those credits reflects the practical versatility expected of supporting radio actors.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves ten Box 13 performances credited to MacDonald, three This Is Your FBI appearances, two each on The Whistler and Yours Truly, Johnny Dollar, and additional work on four other dramatic series.

profiles.name: Joe Cranston
profiles.excerpt: Joe Cranston built a radio and television acting career before expanding into screenwriting and film production, decades before his son Bryan became a major actor.
profiles.bio_html:
Joseph Louis Cranston was born in Chicago in 1924 and pursued acting in Hollywood during the 1950s. Radio westerns and crime drama gave him steady supporting work before film and television became the larger focus of his career.

Cranston later moved behind the camera as a screenwriter and producer, with credits including Trauma and The Crawling Hand. Those activities were substantial professional work, so writing and production remain genuine secondary categories alongside acting.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves nine Gunsmoke performances credited to Cranston, six Fort Laramie appearances, three Have Gun, Will Travel episodes and additional work on Barrie Craig, Escape and The Six Shooter.

profiles.name: Lloyd Battista
profiles.excerpt: Lloyd Battista brought Broadway and screen experience into CBS Radio Mystery Theater while also building a parallel career as a screenwriter.
profiles.bio_html:
Lloyd Battista was born in Cleveland in 1937 and trained at the Carnegie Institute of Technology before building a career on Broadway, television and film. His screen work ranged from American television to European westerns and later character roles.

Battista became a recurring performer on CBS Radio Mystery Theater during the network revival of the 1970s and 1980s. He also worked professionally as a screenwriter, including scripts connected to the Tony Anthony films, making writing a substantial second branch of his career.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves 21 CBS Radio Mystery Theater performances credited to Battista. Those broadcasts document the radio-drama side of a career that moved freely between acting and writing.

profiles.name: J. Pat O'Malley
profiles.excerpt: J. Pat O'Malley carried a successful British singing career into American radio and became one of Quiet, Please's most frequently used supporting voices.
profiles.bio_html:
J. Pat O'Malley was born in Burnley, England in 1904 and began as a professional singer, recording artist and featured vocalist with Jack Hylton's orchestra. He remained in the United States after touring there and developed a long career in stage, radio, film, television and animation.

Radio made especially good use of O'Malley's command of Irish, Scottish and English voices. He became a frequent supporting actor on Quiet, Please, appearing in more than a dozen broadcasts, and later built an extensive voice career that included major Disney characters. His years as a professional singer remain a genuine second category.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves 15 Quiet, Please performances and six Whitehall 1212 appearances credited under the source form Pat O'Malley. His canonical public name is J. Pat O'Malley to distinguish him from the earlier American film actor of the same surname.

profiles.name: Richard Peel
profiles.excerpt: Richard Peel brought a British stage voice into American radio, becoming a reliable player in Escape, Crime Classics and Suspense before a long television career.
profiles.bio_html:
Richard Peel was born in London in 1920 and established himself as a professional actor before building an American career in radio, film and television. His accent and formal delivery made him particularly useful in historical, literary and international stories.

Radio cast Peel repeatedly on Escape, Crime Classics and Suspense. Those programs drew heavily on actors who could establish period and place immediately through voice, and Peel's British background gave him a natural place in that repertory.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves ten Escape performances credited to Peel, six Crime Classics appearances, three Sears Radio Theater episodes and two Suspense broadcasts.

profiles.name: Roy Glenn
profiles.excerpt: Roy Glenn was a pioneering Black radio and screen character actor whose five-decade career stretched from network comedy and drama to Guess Who's Coming to Dinner.
profiles.bio_html:
Roy Glenn was born in Pittsburg, Kansas in 1914 and began professional acting during an era when Black performers faced severe limitations in American broadcasting and film. Radio became one of the first places where his strong voice and authority could sustain a long working career.

Glenn appeared on programs ranging from Amos 'n' Andy and The Jack Benny Program to serious crime and suspense drama. His later screen work included A Raisin in the Sun and a memorable role as Sidney Poitier's father in Guess Who's Coming to Dinner.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves eight Yours Truly, Johnny Dollar performances credited to Glenn, four Tales of the Texas Rangers appearances, three Broadway Is My Beat episodes, two each on CBS Radio Workshop and Suspense, and additional dramatic work.

profiles.name: Alfred Shirley
profiles.excerpt: Alfred Shirley was a veteran New York radio actor whose surviving credits range from Mercury Theatre productions to wartime drama and early science fiction.
profiles.bio_html:
Alfred Shirley belonged to the New York radio repertory that supplied dramatic programs with experienced stage voices across the 1930s, 1940s and 1950s. Personal biography is less complete than his surviving broadcast record, but that record spans several important eras of network drama.

Shirley appeared on The Mercury Theatre on the Air, Columbia Workshop, Words at War and later X Minus One. That progression carried him from experimental literary radio and wartime programming into the science-fiction boom of the 1950s.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves five The Mercury Theatre on the Air performances credited to Shirley, two each on Columbia Workshop, Words at War and X Minus One, plus additional work on Dangerously Yours, Matinee Theater and Top Secret.
